reference_drawer.title: 📖 HCF & LCM Formula & Theorem Guide
reference_drawer.description: Essential formulas and definitions for HCF and LCM calculations:

items.rule: Product of the smallest (minimum) powers of each common prime factor involved in the numbers.
items.formula: \begin{aligned} \text{HCF} &= \text{Product of smallest powers} \\ &\quad \text{of common prime factors} \end{aligned}

items.rule: Product of the greatest (maximum) powers of every prime factor involved in the numbers.
items.formula: \begin{aligned} \text{LCM} &= \text{Product of greatest powers} \\ &\quad \text{of all prime factors} \end{aligned}

items.rule: The product of HCF and LCM equals the product of the two original numbers.
The product relationship HCF × LCM = a × b × c is NOT valid for 3 or more numbers.
items.formula: \text{HCF}(a, b, c) \times \text{LCM}(a, b, c) \neq a \times b \times c

items.rule: Meeting again, repeating bells, circular tracks → LCM. Maximum container capacity, largest stack, dividing into equal heaps → HCF.

concepts.title: 1. What is HCF (Highest Common Factor)?
concepts.subtitle: Common Prime Factors with Smallest Exponents
concepts.summary: HCF is the largest positive integer that divides all the given numbers without leaving a remainder.

points.text: Definition: The greatest common divisor that divides all given numbers (2, 3, or more numbers) exactly.
Factorisation Rule: Take ONLY the prime factors that are common to all numbers, raised to their smallest (minimum) powers.

concepts.trap: Never include non-common primes in HCF.

concepts.title: 2. What is LCM (Lowest Common Multiple)?
concepts.subtitle: All Prime Factors with Greatest Exponents
concepts.summary: LCM is the smallest positive integer that is divisible by all given numbers.

points.text: Definition: The smallest positive common multiple divisible by each of the given numbers (2, 3, or more numbers).
Factorisation Rule: Take every prime factor appearing in ANY of the numbers, raised to its greatest (maximum) power.

concepts.trap: Do not leave out non-common primes when computing LCM.

concepts.title: 3. The Two-Number Identity Bridge
concepts.subtitle: HCF × LCM = a × b (Strictly for Two Numbers Only)
concepts.summary: For any two positive integers a and b, the product of their HCF and LCM is equal to their product.

points.text: Important Limitation: This formula does NOT work for 3 or more numbers: $\text{HCF}(a,b,c) \times \text{LCM}(a,b,c) \neq a \times b \times c$.

concepts.trap: Never use HCF × LCM = a × b × c for 3 or more numbers!

concepts.title: 4. CBSE Board Exam Typology & Blueprints
concepts.subtitle: 4 Standard Problem Types in CBSE Board Exams
concepts.summary: Every exam question from this topic is based on one of these 4 standard models:

points.text:
Type 1: Two-Number HCF, LCM & Verification
Find HCF & LCM of 2 numbers and verify $\text{HCF} \times \text{LCM} = a \times b$.

Type 2: Three-Number Factorisation
Compute HCF & LCM for 3 numbers (e.g. 12, 15, 21) using prime powers.

Type 3: Finding Unknown via Formula
Given $\text{HCF}(306, 657) = 9$, find LCM directly via $\text{LCM} = \frac{a \times b}{\text{HCF}}$.

Type 4: Real-World Word Problems
Circular track / interval bells (LCM) vs container capacity / stacks (HCF).

Because we need the smallest divisor of 18 and 12

option_details.text: Because the meeting time must be a common multiple of both round times (divisible by 18 and 12)
option_details.explanation: Correct! They meet at multiples of their round times, so the first meeting requires the Least Common Multiple.

option_details.text: Because we need the smallest divisor of 18 and 12
option_details.explanation: A divisor would be less than 12 minutes, which is impossible since neither has finished a round.

option_details.text: Because they are driving in opposite directions
option_details.explanation: The problem states they go in the same direction.
The mathematical reason is synchronous repeating periods (LCM).
